newsitem.title: UK: Ex-UK air cargo discounting resisted by national cuts.
newsitem.headline: Ex-UK air cargo discounting resisted by national cuts.

text.p: Some combined passenger/cargo carriers are cutting rates in order to grab market share although dedicated freight carriers and premium carriers are filling their planes, a Reuters survey showed.
Some of this rate cutting has been seen on prime routes but Tony Edwards,UK and ireland cargo manager at Japan Airlines said that his problem has been a lack of space.
"Space has been our priority and March has started well and is filling fast with our three times a week 747-200F freighter flights fully booked until March 26 week," he added.
Edwards said imports into Japan were boosted by firms using up remaining funds in budgets before the end of the the financial year.

British Airways has extended to March 16 its February reductions adding seven Asian routes to the 53 worldwide which formed its February "sale" partially reflecting the seasonally quiet first quarter.
Some cargo carriers said that without passenger revenue they cannot match the cut prices available for combined carriers and doubted the economics of these rates in anything but the short-term.
Other major combination carriers said they are selling a service and are simply not prepared to match the prices being offered by BA.

In addition to the extra destinations BA made further reductions in some pallet and bin rates in its February promotion. Industry sources said some of the BA promotional rates gave them a price advantage of one third against comparable pallet rates.

Some carriers refused to compete with BA on their home routes but forwarders said others were more aggressive and dropped spot rates. Several airline sources said they were being heavily undercut on their home routes by carriers offering very cheap indirect flights or by forwarders passing on the pallet rate reductions.
This meant some shippers were able to take advantage of rates of only a fraction of the premium direct flights offered by national carriers although often only on one off negotiation.

The Indian sub-continent suffered particularly from rate cutting with forwarders buying discounted pallets and then grabbing business by passing on the reduced rates. Carriers said this meant it was possible to fly 100 kilo packages to Bombay and Delhi at just over 30 pence a kilo against average market rates of some 75 and 65 pence respectively.

Most but not by any means all airlines have announced rate increases to come into force at or close to the summer schedules start date of April one. But the durability of some of these increases has been questioned by BA's special discounts which apply until March 16 or the day before BA lifts its rates by up to ten percent - its Asian rates climb seven percent.
One competitor to described this effort to lift rates immediately after a cut price promotion as "wishful thinking".

A mixed outlook was painted by Korean Air Lines manager Frank Smith who said improving activity but described business "as the usual sort of commercial traffic". Demand has improved but is still behind the same time last year and is more erratic.
"But I think it could be a reasonable year (for KAL) despite the slowdown in Chinese imports," Smith added.
A highlight yet to come in traffic to Korea later this year may be the building of a new national horse stud which could require over 200 racehorses to be flown from Ireland to Korea, Smith said.

The strength of sterling could pose a threat to British exports later this year and some forwarders caution this could damage ex-UK air freight business later this year. But carriers said the rise of sterling has not priced the UK out of the air freight market as previously ex-UK rates were underpriced against Euiropean equivalents.
Although the cost of jet fuel has slipped it is not yet back to the level where a relaxation of the fuel surcharge is imminent.
A background talking point has been the stance taken by Air Canada to combat the problem of no shows - when a forwarder or shipper fails to present cargo for shipment despite making a firm booking.

The debate hinges on the inter-responsibility of the service provided by carriers and forwarders and what their clients the shippers expect. It is also being conducted in the UK Air Freight Forum - a tripartite talking shop established late last year.

Some carriers said recent rate cutting has increased the problem of no shows as some forwarders and their shipper customers are unable to resist the low rates made available via the cut price pallet rates. Larger forwarders distanced themselves from this preferring stable long term relationships with carriers.
KAL's Smith said the advent of open skies and extra competition means that carriers cannot afford to fly empty planes making the long standing issue of no shows very topical.

Andrew Traill, manager for shipping and air at British Freight Transport Association (FTA) which helped establish the Forum said he was sure other carriers would follow Air Canada's example as it is quite reasonable to ask for advance warning of a cancelled cargo.
The issue had already come up at the Forum and some shippers had been unaware of the problems caused at carriers, he added.
Now the industry must decide how to tackle the problem and how to measure its extent.

There has been widespread support from other airlines for Air Canada which is only penalising weekend no shows as airlines are at their most vulnerable then with little chance of obtaining substitute cargoes. Other airlines may well follow, industry sources said.
KAL's Smith was one who described as "brave" Air Canada's move to impose penalties on no shows. A carrier taking a tough stance risks losing business.

For some months Air Hong Kong and Emirates have operated similar schemes on larger packages. Both have tied their agents or forwarders to contracts stipulating that penalties be paid for no shows although neither have had to impose penalties as yet.
What it has meant is that permanent bookings are more closely monitored and are reduced where necessary.

No shows at Air Hong Kong face a 50 percent of fees on agents or forwarders who do not give 72 hours notice of not taking up booked space of 10 tonnes or more and applies to all flights, said Air Hong Kong UK manager Bob Wetherill.

Emirates' imposes a variable penalty for no shows on bookings of over 4.5 tonnes of 25 percent if cancelled less than three days in advance, 50 percent under two days ahead and 75 percent with less than a day's notice, said Emirates cargo manager Ray Disson.
Emirates lost a total of 125 tonnes of valuable pre-booked cargo space in December as a result of no shows on smaller packages.

It is now looking at a similar scheme for smaller packages and Disson said it would be reasonable for such contract penalties to work both ways with airlines facing penalties for failing to fly cargo as booked. But such contracts are still only in the design stage.
Air Hong Kong will be returning to five 740-200F's a week to Hong Kong from Manchester in mid-April after a reduction to four made in October, said Wetherill.
As a result of the winter capacity reduction, Wetherill said Air Hong Kong has filled its flights and is implementing a fare rise of 10 percent on April one.

Earlier this week Lufthansa underlined its position of maintaining tripartite discussions with forwarders and shippers and reckons this emphasis on long-term relationships has promoted demand analysis and minimised no shows.

But Thai Airways International Ltd's UK and Ireland cargo manager Mike Miller said most of its Asian ex-UK rates were rising five percent in April with a capacity shortage lifting rates to Perth by an exceptional 9.5 percent; another exception is Viewnam where rates being cut. Emirates lifts its rates by five percent on April one while Lufthansa's rates to the MidEast and Asia rise by an average of five percent next month.

Malaysian Airline System Bhd reduced cargo capacity ex-UK this week when it gave up flying a 747 combi in favour of a passenger 747 offering only bellyhold cargo space. Its ex-UK rates rise by between 5 and 20 percent from April 1.

Both Philippine Airlines and KAL are keeping rates unchanged and Philippines UK cargo manager Keith O'Callaghan said it would look again at rates in six months and cited BA's rate cutting as key factor in deterring it from raising rates now.
Philippine Airlines are "fairly busy with planes going out full" with just occasional spot rating taking 5 or 10 pence off rates on an ad hoc basis, O'Callaghan said.
Singapore Airlines is raising some selected rates by 3-5 percent on April one but leaving main routes unchanged.

Thai Airlines's Miller said one firm spot has been to Kathmandu where it reckons to have some 20 percent of an air cargo import market dominated by high tech goods. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsreel Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
